claim: Set up dedicated reference-image viewport panes (UV/Image Editor windows split beside the 3D viewport, not just background images inside it) showing multiple reference photos side-by-side (e.g. one for silhouette/proportions, one for surface/material detail) -- when reference photos of the same real-world object type disagree with each other, explicitly choose one specific reference to follow for primary proportions while treating the others as secondary detail/material reference, rather than trying to average or reconcile them.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation (2026-08-14, watched full video): at 2:14-2:58, the viewport is split with dedicated UV/Image Editor panes showing multiple anvil reference photos side by side, with one chosen as the primary proportions reference and others used for material/wear detail.
rejected_alternative: Modeling from memory, or trying to average/reconcile conflicting reference photos into one blended proportion set

claim: When blocking out a complex form with both simple and organic/curved sections (e.g. an anvil's flat rectangular base versus its curved horn and waist), start from the single most unambiguous planar/symmetrical primitive shape (here, the flat rectangular base footprint) and build outward into the more complex curved transitions -- not from the curved sections first, where dimensions and orientation are inherently ambiguous.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation: at 4:06-4:35, the flat rectangular base footprint (the least ambiguous shape in the reference) is identified and blocked out first, before any of the anvil's curved horn/waist sections are touched.
rejected_alternative: Starting the blockout from a curved/organic section of the form
reason: A simple planar shape has unambiguous dimensions and orientation to establish first; starting with a curved section risks compounding uncertainty into every later step.

claim: Deliberately demonstrated anti-pattern: building a tapered/curved transition (e.g. a stepped pyramid shape) via manual repeated extrude-then-scale steps produces uneven edge-loop spacing, non-uniform curvature, and imprecise tapering that's hard to smooth out afterward. The correct approach: extrude the full height as one clean primitive first, THEN subdivide it uniformly (evenly-spaced loop cuts) -- shape the taper by manipulating the uniform loops afterward, not by varying the extrusion/scale amount at each step.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation: at 5:07-5:40, repeated manual extrude-then-scale steps are shown deliberately producing an uneven, stepped pyramid with inconsistent ring spacing, presented as the intuitive-but-wrong approach.
rejected_alternative: Building a tapered form step-by-step via repeated extrude-then-scale operations
reason: Manually varying extrusion/scale amount at each step compounds spacing inconsistency; extruding the full form first and then subdividing uniformly separates the 'how much geometry' decision from the 'what shape' decision.

claim: Before applying any deformation (modifiers, proportional editing, lattices) to a tall extruded section, pre-divide it into evenly-spaced loop cuts (Ctrl+R with scroll-wheel count) first -- uneven vertex distribution going into a deformation step causes the resulting surface to buckle, crease, or pinch unevenly, regardless of how good the deformation tool itself is.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation: at 6:06-6:40, a tall extrusion is pre-divided into 12 evenly-spaced horizontal loop cuts specifically to give any later deformation operation a uniform grid to work with.
rejected_alternative: Deforming a section that still has uneven/sparse loop-cut spacing

claim: To narrow/taper a cross-section (e.g. an anvil's waist) purely in its horizontal silhouette without compressing the vertical spacing between its loops: enable Proportional Editing (O) with the desired falloff curve (Inverse Square gives a natural concave flare; Sphere, Linear, Random are the alternatives cycled through), then scale with S followed by Shift+Z to lock the Z axis out of the transform -- only the X/Y (horizontal) extent changes while exact layer heights are preserved.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation: at 6:50-8:48, an edge loop is scaled with Proportional Editing and S then Shift+Z, constraining the taper to the horizontal plane only and preserving exact vertical layer heights, with the falloff curve cycled to compare Inverse Square/Linear/Random/Sphere results.
rejected_alternative: Scaling with a plain S, which compresses vertical spacing along with the horizontal taper

claim: Proportional Editing's radius affects every vertex within range regardless of whether it should stay rigid -- when a nearby flat/rigid surface (e.g. a flat top deck) is unintentionally warped by a proportional-editing deformation targeting an adjacent curved section, temporarily Hide (H) the geometry meant to stay rigid before performing the deformation, then Unhide (Alt+H) afterward -- this removes it from the proportional-editing falloff calculation entirely without needing a vertex group mask.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation: at 11:38-12:25, a flat top deck being unintentionally dragged by proportional editing targeting an adjacent curved horn section is fixed by hiding the flat deck's vertices (H), performing the deformation, then unhiding (Alt+H).
rejected_alternative: Setting up a vertex group mask to exclude the rigid surface from proportional editing's influence
reason: Hiding is a faster, simpler way to exclude specific geometry from a proportional-editing operation's influence than setting up a formal vertex group mask for a one-off deformation.

claim: Periodically step back and evaluate the whole object's silhouette and apparent center of gravity against the reference image, rather than only checking individual features/sections in isolation -- a section that looks individually correct in close-up detail work (e.g. a waist section) can still make the overall object read as too tall/top-heavy compared to the reference, a problem only visible from the full silhouette view.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation: at 12:40-13:18, stepping back to compare the whole model's silhouette against the reference reveals the waist section is too tall relative to the reference's squat, heavy base, prompting a global scale correction (0.70) that individual-feature work hadn't caught.
rejected_alternative: Only evaluating each feature/section in isolation as it's built, without periodic full-silhouette comparison
reason: Feature-level correctness doesn't guarantee correct overall proportions; only a full silhouette comparison against the reference catches drift in the object's overall weight/proportion.
